stem: A used-car market has 600 buyers, each willing to buy at most one car, and 500 sellers, each owning one car. There are 400 good cars (peaches) and 100 bad cars (lemons). Buyers value a peach at Rs.100 and a lemon at Rs.10. Sellers value their own peach at Rs.50 or their own lemon at Rs.10. Sellers know their car's quality; buyers know only the aggregate numbers and all valuations. What outcome maximizes aggregate surplus? Explain. [4 marks]
answer: Trade all 400 peaches; lemon trade is optional. Maximum gains from trade are Rs.20,000.
solution:
Efficiency concerns which cars are traded when their qualities are known, not the price paid for them. A good car creates surplus equal to the buyer’s valuation minus the current owner’s value. A lemon creates no gain from trade at the specified equal values. Transfers cancel from total welfare, so identify all positive-gain trades and count them, while treating zero-gain trades as optional in the efficient set.

Trading a peach generates a gain of $100-50=50$, while trading a lemon generates $10-10=0$. There are enough buyers to buy all 500 cars, so no beneficial peach transaction needs to be crowded out by another trade.

Thus every peach should move from its seller to a buyer, generating $400\cdot50=20{,}000$. Any number of lemons may also trade without changing aggregate gains from trade.

This is the gains-from-trade surplus, relative to sellers retaining their cars.

stem: A used-car market has 600 buyers, each willing to buy at most one car, and 500 sellers, each owning one car. There are 400 good cars (peaches) and 100 bad cars (lemons). Buyers value a peach at Rs.100 and a lemon at Rs.10. Sellers value their own peach at Rs.50 or their own lemon at Rs.10. Sellers know their car's quality; buyers know only the aggregate numbers and all valuations. (i) Derive the supply of used cars as a function of price, and draw it with quantity on the horizontal axis and price on the vertical axis. (ii) Derive and draw demand in the same figure. Label all important points. (iii) Find all competitive equilibria and identify the qualities traded. [20 marks]
answer: With weak participation at reservation prices: price 10 with any quantity from 0 to 100 lemons; price 50 with 100 lemons and 80 peaches; or price 82 with all 500 cars.
solution:
With full information, good cars and lemons are separate markets. Buyers can condition their bids on quality, so no pooled expected valuation is needed. Compare demand and supply for each type and retain participation at indifference: when valuation and price coincide, an agent can be willing to trade without strictly preferring it. This is especially relevant for the lemon market, where all possible trades have zero surplus.

Supply is a correspondence: $S(p)=0$ for $p<10$; $S(10)=[0,100]$; $S(p)=100$ for $10<p<50$; $S(50)=[100,500]$; and $S(p)=500$ for $p>50$. Plot horizontal supply segments at prices 10 and 50, with vertical segments at quantities 0, 100 and 500 as appropriate.

Demand must use the quality mix of cars actually offered. A lemon-only pool is worth 10 per car. If all 100 lemons and $k$ peaches are offered, the expected buyer value is $v(k)=(1000+100k)/(100+k)$. For a given pool, demand is 600 below its expected value, zero above it, and any amount in $[0,600]$ at equality. Equivalently, for offered quantity $q>100$, the zero-surplus buyer valuation curve is $p=100-9000/q$, rising from $(q,p)=(100,10)$ to $(500,82)$; for a lemon-only pool it is $p=10$.

At $p=10$, sellers and buyers of lemons are indifferent, so any quantity $q\in[0,100]$ of lemons can clear; if indifference is resolved in favour of full participation, $q=100$. At $p=50$, all lemons are supplied and peach sellers are indifferent. Setting $v(k)=50$ gives $k=80$, so $q=180$ clears. At $p>50$, every car is supplied and expected quality value is $(400\cdot100+100\cdot10)/500=82$. Thus $p=82$, with 500 buyers trading and 100 abstaining, is the full-pooling equilibrium. No other prices clear: on $(10,50)$ only overpriced lemons are offered, and outside these boundary cases demand and supply disagree.
hint: At price 50, peach sellers are indifferent; do not automatically assume all 400 peaches must be offered. Match buyers' expected value to the actual offered pool.
notes: Reservation-price indifference is handled as a correspondence. A convention forcing all indifferent sellers to trade removes the partial-peach equilibrium at p=50 and fixes lemon-only trade at 100. The source does not specify such a tie-breaking convention. Demand is conditional on offered quality, so an unconditional single-valued demand curve is not well-defined without a selection convention.

stem: A used-car market has 600 buyers, each willing to buy at most one car, and 500 sellers, each owning one car. There are 400 good cars (peaches) and 100 bad cars (lemons). Buyers value a peach at Rs.100 and a lemon at Rs.10. Sellers value their own peach at Rs.50 or their own lemon at Rs.10. Sellers know their car's quality; buyers know only the aggregate numbers and all valuations. Now buyers also know each individual car's quality. Use demand and supply analysis to find all competitive equilibria. [6 marks]
answer: All 400 peaches trade at price 100. Lemons have price 10 and any traded quantity in $[0,100]$, under weak participation.
solution:
Under hidden quality, buyers pay for expected quality among cars actually offered, while each seller knows her own type. Thus the seller pool itself depends on price. Solve by price regimes: lemons alone, possible partial entry of good cars at their reservation price, and full entry. At a reservation-price tie, a subset of indifferent sellers may enter, changing expected quality. Ignoring this partial-entry regime can wrongly remove an equilibrium.

With quality observable, buyers can choose peach and lemon markets separately. At a peach price below 100, each of the 600 buyers strictly prefers a peach to abstaining or a fairly priced lemon.

Since there are only 400 peaches, a lower price cannot clear. At price 100 buyers are indifferent and 400 of them can be assigned peaches; all peach sellers strictly prefer selling because 100 exceeds 50.

Thus $p_P=100$, $q_P=400$. In the lemon market both buyer value and seller opportunity cost are 10, so $p_L=10$, with any quantity $q_L\in[0,100]$ under indifference; at most 100 of the remaining 200 buyers are needed.

Full participation gives $q_L=100$. These allocations achieve the efficient Rs.20,000 gains from peach trade.

stem: A private firm $r$ and a public firm $u$ choose nonnegative quantities $q_r,q_u$ of a homogeneous good. Inverse demand is $p=a-bQ$, where $Q=q_r+q_u$, $a,b>0$. Both firms initially have total cost $cq_i$, with $0<c<a$. Derive (i) each firm's profit, (ii) consumer surplus, and (iii) welfare, defined as consumer plus producer surplus. [5 marks]
solution:
Profits include revenue minus each firm’s resource cost; consumer surplus is the area under inverse demand above the market price. When they are added, market payments cancel because what consumers pay is received by firms. This cancellation is why welfare can be written as gross benefit minus total production cost and depends only on total Q when both firms have the same marginal cost.

Revenue minus cost gives $\pi_r=(a-b(q_r+q_u)-c)q_r$ and $\pi_u=(a-b(q_r+q_u)-c)q_u$. The area below inverse demand and above market price is $CS=\int_0^Q(a-bz)\,dz-pQ=bQ^2/2$. Adding profits cancels transfers through the price and gives $W=\int_0^Q(a-bz)\,dz-cQ=(a-c)Q-bQ^2/2$.
hint: Consumer surplus is a triangle; total welfare equals gross willingness to pay minus production cost.

Both firms initially have total cost $cq_i$, with $0<c<a$. For given $q_u$, set up the private firm's profit maximization problem and derive its reaction function. [3 marks]
solution:
A best response optimizes only the private firm’s output while taking public output as fixed. Its extra output earns revenue on that unit but also lowers the price on its existing units. This gives the factor two on its own quantity in the first-order condition. Because a negative output is infeasible, truncate the interior response at zero; the reaction curve is a line segment plus a corner segment, not a whole unbounded line.

The private firm solves $\max_{q_r\geq0}(a-c-bq_u-bq_r)q_r$. The interior first-order condition is $a-c-bq_u-2bq_r=0$, and the second derivative is $-2b<0$. Enforcing nonnegativity yields $BR_r(q_u)=\max\{(a-c-bq_u)/(2b),0\}$.
hint: Differentiate private profit with respect to $q_r$, holding $q_u$ fixed.

Both firms initially have total cost $cq_i$, with $0<c<a$. For given $q_r$, set up the public firm's welfare maximization problem and derive its reaction function. [3 marks]
solution:
The public firm maximizes total welfare, so its price effect on the other firm is not an external loss in the same way as in private profit maximization: price transfers cancel. Its extra output is valuable until demand price equals the common marginal resource cost. Therefore it supplies the gap between the efficient total output and the private firm’s chosen amount, unless that gap is negative, in which case its best response is zero.

The public firm solves $\max_{q_u\geq0}(a-c)(q_r+q_u)-\frac b2(q_r+q_u)^2$. Its interior first-order condition is $a-c-b(q_r+q_u)=0$; the second derivative is $-b<0$. Therefore $BR_u(q_r)=\max\{(a-c)/b-q_r,0\}$.

Both firms initially have total cost $cq_i$, with $0<c<a$. Define equilibrium under quantity competition, find equilibrium outputs, price, profits, consumer surplus and welfare, and illustrate it using reaction functions with $q_u$ on the horizontal axis and $q_r$ on the vertical axis. [11 marks]
answer: $q_r^*=0$, $q_u^*=(a-c)/b$, $p^*=c$, both profits zero, and $CS^*=W^*=(a-c)^2/(2b)$.
solution:
An equilibrium is an intersection of the complete reaction correspondences, including zero-output corners. Solving just two interior equalities may yield a boundary and does not by itself rule out another corner. Check the public-output-zero case separately. The public firm’s welfare objective ultimately eliminates the private markup, driving total output to the efficient quantity; at that price the private firm’s best response can be zero even though the market is active.

A Nash equilibrium is a pair of quantities at which neither firm can improve its objective by changing its own quantity while holding the other's fixed. Put $A=(a-c)/b>0$.

The reactions are $q_r=\max\{(A-q_u)/2,0\}$ and $q_u=\max\{A-q_r,0\}$. If the public output is positive, substituting $q_u=A-q_r$ into the private reaction gives $q_r=q_r/2$, hence $q_r=0$ and $q_u=A$.

A corner with $q_u=0$ cannot be an equilibrium because the private best response is $A/2$, at which the public firm wants $A/2>0$. Thus the stated equilibrium is unique.

Total output is $A$, price is $a-bA=c$, and each firm's margin and profit are zero. Consumer surplus and welfare are $bA^2/2=(a-c)^2/(2b)$.

In the requested graph the private reaction joins $(0,A/2)$ to $(A,0)$ before lying along the horizontal axis; the positive public reaction is the line from $(0,A)$ to $(A,0)$. Their equilibrium intersection is $(q_u,q_r)=(A,0)$.

stem: A private firm $r$ and a public firm $u$ choose nonnegative quantities $q_r,q_u$ of a homogeneous good. Inverse demand is $p=a-bQ$, where $Q=q_r+q_u$, $a,b>0$. Both firms initially have total cost $cq_i$, with $0<c<a$. The private firm's marginal cost falls to $c_r<c$, while public marginal cost remains $c$. Draw the new reaction functions and explain how $q_r,q_u,Q$, price, both profits, consumer surplus and welfare change. Exact expressions are not required. [8 marks]
answer: Private output and profit rise; public output falls (possibly to zero). Total output and consumer surplus weakly rise, price weakly falls, public profit remains zero, and welfare rises.
solution:
The public reaction depends on its own marginal cost, which stays c, while the private reaction moves as its cost falls. Initially the public firm can substitute away from its own production one for one, keeping the efficient total and price unchanged. That adjustment cannot continue below zero public output. A large enough cost reduction crosses this corner and leaves a private monopoly, so the comparative statics must distinguish small and large cost changes rather than extrapolate one interior regime.

The public reaction remains $q_u=\max\{(a-c)/b-q_r,0\}$, because the effect of its own output on welfare is still $p-c$. The private reaction shifts upward to $q_r=\max\{(a-c_r-bq_u)/(2b),0\}$. Let $\delta=c-c_r>0$ and $A=(a-c)/b$. If $\delta\leq a-c$, the intersection is $q_r=\delta/b$ and $q_u=A-\delta/b$. Thus output shifts from the public firm to the cheaper private firm while $Q=A$, $p=c$ and consumer surplus remain unchanged. Private profit becomes $\delta^2/b>0$, public profit remains zero, and welfare rises by the production-cost saving $\delta^2/b$.

If the cost fall is so large that $\delta>a-c$, the public firm reaches its zero-output corner. The private firm then produces $(a-c_r)/(2b)>A$ and charges $(a+c_r)/2<c$. Total output and consumer surplus rise strictly; private profit and welfare rise, while public profit remains zero because its output is zero. The second regime matters because the question does not restrict the size of the cost reduction.

stem: A unit mass of consumers each buys at most one unit. Consumer valuation $v$ is uniform on $[0,1]$. A monopoly has total cost $q^3$ and initially cannot identify consumers, so must set one uniform price. Derive demand as a function of price. [6 marks]
answer: $q(p)=1$ for $p\leq0$, $q(p)=1-p$ for $0<p<1$, and $q(p)=0$ for $p\geq1$.
solution:
Each consumer chooses at most one unit, so market demand is the mass of consumers whose valuation reaches the posted price. For a uniform distribution this mass is the length of the valuation interval above p. The total population is normalized to one, making the mass and interval length numerically equal. Truncate at the endpoints because a quantity above one or below zero cannot be demanded.

A consumer buys when $v\geq p$. For $0<p<1$, the uniform distribution puts mass $1-p$ above $p$, so demand is $1-p$.

At a nonpositive price all consumers buy, while a price at least 1 generates zero demand except for a measure-zero indifferent endpoint. Economically relevant nonnegative prices therefore give inverse demand $p=1-q$ for $0\leq q\leq1$.

solution:
Use inverse demand to express both revenue and cost in q. The cost is total cost q³, so its marginal cost is 3q²; using q³ directly as marginal cost would produce a different answer. The profit derivative has a feasible positive root and an infeasible negative root. Check the second derivative over the full feasible interval, not just at the candidate, to establish that the positive root is the unique global maximum.

Using inverse demand, profit is $\pi(q)=(1-q)q-q^3$. The first derivative is $1-2q-3q^2$, which vanishes at $q=1/3$ (the other root is -1).

The second derivative $-2-6q$ is strictly negative on $[0,1]$, so this is the unique maximum. Consequently $p=1-q=2/3$ and $\pi=2/9-1/27=5/27$.

stem: A unit mass of consumers each buys at most one unit. Consumer valuation $v$ is uniform on $[0,1]$. A monopoly has total cost $q^3$ and initially cannot identify consumers, so must set one uniform price. For a cost the firm can learn whether a consumer's valuation is in $[0,4/5]$ or in $(4/5,1]$. What is the maximum amount it is willing to pay for this information? Explain. [20 marks]
answer: The maximum payment is $(46\sqrt{115}-472)/675\approx0.0315482$.
solution:
Information permits two group-specific prices, but not individualized perfect discrimination within each group. Group quantities are actual population masses, so the high group has a strict capacity of one fifth. Build inverse demands for those masses and subtract the shared cost of total output once. If unconstrained first-order conditions ask for more high buyers than exist, the optimum lies on a group-demand boundary. The value of information is the increase in optimized profit, not the entire informed profit.

With information the firm can price separately to the two groups. Let $l\in[0,4/5]$ and $h\in[0,1/5]$ be quantities sold to the low- and high-valuation groups. Inverse group demands are $p_L=4/5-l$ and $p_H=1-h$. The profit objective is $(4/5-l)l+(1-h)h-(l+h)^3$, a strictly concave function over the rectangle of feasible quantities.

An unrestricted interior solution would require $4/5-2l=1-2h=3(l+h)^2$. It gives $h>1/5$, which is infeasible. The optimum therefore serves the entire high group: $h=1/5$, at $p_H=4/5$. If $Q=l+1/5$, the remaining first-order condition is $4/5-2l=3Q^2$, or $3Q^2+2Q-6/5=0$. Thus $Q=(\sqrt{115}-5)/15$ and $l=(\sqrt{115}-8)/15$. Low-group price is $p_L=1-Q=(20-\sqrt{115})/15$. The high-group marginal revenue at its upper quantity is $3/5$, exceeding marginal cost $3Q^2$, as required for this boundary optimum. Substitution yields informed profit $(46\sqrt{115}-347)/675\approx0.2167334$. Subtracting the uninformed profit $5/27$ gives the willingness to pay $(46\sqrt{115}-472)/675\approx0.0315482$.

Each of the $\bar L$ workers supplies one unit if $W>\bar W$, supplies none if $W<\bar W$, and is indifferent at equality. Aggregate demand is a standard downward-sloping curve. Derive aggregate labour supply as a function of nominal wage $W$. [4 marks]
answer: $L^S(W)=0$ below $\bar W$, $[0,\bar L]$ at $\bar W$, and $\bar L$ above $\bar W$.

Every worker has the same reservation nominal wage. Below it nobody supplies labour; above it everyone supplies their endowed unit. At the reservation wage, indifference permits any quantity between those extremes, so labour supply is a correspondence there. This distinction is important because equilibrium at that wage can have partial employment. Replacing the indifferent segment by an arbitrary single quantity would remove legitimate equilibria.

answer: Desired labour is zero if $W/P>A$, arbitrary nonnegative if $W/P=A$, and unbounded if $W/P<A$; in nominal terms compare $W$ with $PA$.
solution:
The production function is linear in labour, so the marginal product A does not diminish. Consequently competitive profit is linear in the amount hired. Away from the zero-margin wage there is no interior labour first-order condition selecting a finite desired quantity: the firm either hires none or wants unbounded labour in an unconstrained problem. The workforce limit constrains equilibrium supply, not the firm’s technological desire for workers at a profitable wage.

The labour-dependent part of competitive profit is $(PA-W)L$. If $W/P>A$, every extra worker loses money, so desired employment is zero.

If $W/P=A$, every nonnegative employment level yields the same labour profit. If $W/P<A$, the linear technology gives a positive constant profit per extra worker and hence no finite unconstrained maximizer: desired labour is unbounded.

The finite workforce constrains realized equilibrium employment, not unconstrained desired labour. For a fixed price level, replace the comparison $W/P$ versus $A$ with $W$ versus $PA$.

The inverse labour-demand curve is horizontal at $W=PA$.

answer: $L^*=0$ if $P<\bar W/A$, $L^*\in[0,\bar L]$ at equality, and $L^*=\bar L$ if $P>\bar W/A$.
solution:
In the nominal-wage diagram, labour demand is horizontal at the value marginal product PA. Compare that height with the workers’ reservation wage. Below it, no positive employment can satisfy both sides; above it, the full workforce clears at the value marginal product. At exact equality, both the firm and workers are indifferent over a range, which creates the continuum of employment levels. Keep this equality case when deriving the price-dependent supply relation.

For fixed $P$, inverse demand is the horizontal line $W=PA$. Supply is horizontal at $\bar W$ over $0\leq L\leq\bar L$ and vertical at the full workforce above that wage.

If $PA<\bar W$, no mutually acceptable wage supports positive labour: firms will not pay the reservation wage, and workers will not accept their marginal revenue product. Equilibrium employment is zero.

If $PA>\bar W$, labour-market clearing requires $W=PA$ and all $\bar L$ workers are employed. If $PA=\bar W$, both sides are indifferent, so any employment between 0 and $\bar L$ clears at that wage.

These are the stated cases after dividing by $A>0$.

answer: Demand expansion raises output on the horizontal AS segment, but raises only prices on either vertical segment until a regime boundary is reached.
solution:
Demand policy shifts AD but the amount of resulting output adjustment depends on which AS segment it meets. On a horizontal AS segment, the price is pinned and output adjusts. On a vertical segment, capacity or the wage threshold fixes output and price adjusts. Describe all three regimes because a low-output state below the reservation-price threshold is different from the familiar intermediate Keynesian segment with spare labour at the threshold.

Expansionary monetary or fiscal policy shifts aggregate demand to the right. If equilibrium lies on the horizontal AS segment at $P_0=\bar W/A$ with spare labour, this raises employment and output without changing the price level, until full employment is reached.

If equilibrium is already on the full-employment vertical segment, further expansion raises only the price level. If it lies on the lower-output vertical segment at $Y=\bar K$ with $P<P_0$, a small expansion initially raises only $P$; output begins to increase only when demand is strong enough to bring the price to $P_0$.

Contraction has the reverse regime-dependent effects. Thus it is not correct to state that demand policy always changes output in this model.

stem: In a discrete-time Solow model $Y_t=K_t^\alpha L_t^{1-\alpha}$, $0<\alpha<1$. Competitive factors receive marginal products. Households save a fraction $0<s<1$ of disposable income, and all private savings are invested. There is no depreciation. Labour grows at rate $n>0$. Let $k_t=K_t/L_t$. The government taxes interest earnings at rate $0<\tau<1$, does not tax wages, and spends all tax revenue on consumption. (i) Derive aggregate wage earnings, interest earnings and savings in terms of $Y_t$. (ii) Derive the law of motion for $k_t$. (iii) Find its steady state and its response to $\tau$. [14 marks]
answer: Wages $(1-\alpha)Y_t$, gross interest $\alpha Y_t$, savings $s(1-\tau\alpha)Y_t$; $k_{t+1}=[k_t+s(1-\tau\alpha)k_t^\alpha]/(1+n)$; positive $k^*=[s(1-\tau\alpha)/n]^{1/(1-\alpha)}$, decreasing in $\tau$.
solution:
Competitive factor shares identify the tax base: capital income is alpha times aggregate output, while wages are the remaining share. Taxing only capital returns therefore reduces disposable income by tau alpha Y, not by tau times all output. Because revenue is consumed by the government, none of that amount is added to capital. Derive investment first, then divide next period’s aggregate capital by next period’s labour to obtain the per-worker transition.

The marginal products are $w_t=(1-\alpha)(K_t/L_t)^\alpha$ and $r_t=\alpha(K_t/L_t)^{\alpha-1}$. Thus total wage earnings are $(1-\alpha)Y_t$ and total gross interest earnings are $\alpha Y_t$.

Disposable household income is $(1-\alpha)Y_t+(1-\tau)\alpha Y_t=(1-\tau\alpha)Y_t$, so $S_t=s(1-\tau\alpha)Y_t$. Since tax revenue is consumed rather than invested, $K_{t+1}=K_t+S_t$.

Dividing by $L_{t+1}=(1+n)L_t$ gives $k_{t+1}=[k_t+s(1-\tau\alpha)k_t^\alpha]/(1+n)$. At a positive steady state, $nk^*=s(1-\tau\alpha)(k^*)^\alpha$, yielding the expression above.

Its logarithmic derivative is $\partial\log k^*/\partial\tau=-\alpha/[(1-\alpha)(1-\tau\alpha)]<0$. A higher tax reduces private saving and hence positive steady-state capital.

Zero capital is also an absorbing steady state if admitted; the displayed solution is the economically relevant positive one.

stem: An individual lives for two periods. First-period wage income is $W$, personal savings are $s$, and the gross interest factor is $R>1$. The government takes a first-period lump-sum tax $T$ and returns exactly $T$ in period2. Lifetime utility is $u(c_1)+\beta u(c_2)$, with $0<\beta<1$ and $u$ strictly increasing and strictly concave. Specify the utility maximization problem and budget constraint. Derive the first-order condition and interpret it economically. [9 marks]
answer: Maximize $u(W-T-s)+\beta u(Rs+T)$ over feasible saving; an interior optimum satisfies $u'(c_1)=\beta R u'(c_2)$.
solution:
The government scheme shifts T rupees forward without paying interest. Its present value is therefore less than the first-period tax, so the policy is not a pure timing change at an unchanged lifetime wealth. Write both period budgets before differentiating. One additional privately saved rupee lowers present consumption by one and raises future consumption by R, producing the Euler condition. Borrowing or consumption constraints require inequalities if they bind.

The two period budgets are $c_1=W-T-s$ and $c_2=Rs+T$. Equivalently $c_1+c_2/R=W-T+T/R$.

Choose $s$ to maximize $u(W-T-s)+\beta u(Rs+T)$ subject to nonnegative consumption (and $s\geq0$ if borrowing is disallowed). Differentiating at an interior optimum gives $-u'(W-T-s)+\beta R u'(Rs+T)=0$.

Strict concavity makes an interior solution unique. The condition equates the marginal utility lost by saving one additional first-period rupee to the discounted utility gained from its $R$ rupees of second-period consumption.

At a binding constraint a one-sided/KKT inequality replaces the equality.

answer: The claim does not follow from the stated assumptions and is false in general. Log utility gives the opposite ranking.
solution:
The request is a universal claim under general concave utility. Before differentiating a complicated expression, test it using a simple admissible utility such as log consumption. If the direction reverses in one feasible interior example, no proof of the printed universal statement is possible. The key danger in a general derivative is that curvature terms are evaluated at optimal consumption, which itself changes with beta; they cannot be treated as fixed constants when comparing different individuals.

Take the permitted utility $u(c)=\log c$ and an interior solution. The Euler equation gives $s=\beta W/(1+\beta)-(\beta R+1)T/[R(1+\beta)]$.

Therefore $ds/dT=-(\beta R+1)/[R(1+\beta)]$. The derivative of its absolute magnitude with respect to $\beta$ is $(R-1)/[R(1+\beta)^2]>0$.

Thus a larger discount factor (less myopia), not a smaller one, produces the larger absolute cut in saving in this example. For example $R=2,W=10,T=1$ yields interior savings at both $\beta=1/4$ and $\beta=1/2$; the crowding-out magnitudes are $3/5$ and $2/3$, respectively.

More myopia therefore yields a smaller cut. In general, the curvatures $u''(c_1)$ and $u''(c_2)$ in part(c) are evaluated at consumption levels that also change with $\beta$, so one cannot hold them fixed to infer the comparative static requested here.

Additional restrictions, or a corrected claim, are necessary.

stem: Let $C=\{(x,y):0\leq x\leq1,\ 0\leq y\leq1,\ y\leq x\}$ and maximize $ax+by$ over $C$. For $a\neq0$ and $b\neq0$, show that an optimal solution can be chosen from $(0,0),(1,0),(1,1)$. Describe all coefficient values for which each vertex is optimal. [20 marks]
answer: $(0,0)$ is optimal iff $a\leq0$ and $a+b\leq0$; $(1,0)$ iff $a\geq0$ and $b\leq0$; $(1,1)$ iff $b\geq0$ and $a+b\geq0$, subject to the stated nonzero coefficients.
solution:
A linear objective over a triangle attains a maximum at some vertex, but may have other optimal points on an edge. Express every feasible point as a convex combination of the three vertices to prove the vertex assertion without assuming a general linear-programming theorem. Then compare the three vertex objective values 0,a,a+b. Use weak inequalities for a vertex to be an optimizer and strict inequalities when claiming it is the unique optimizer.

The feasible set is the triangle with vertices $(0,0),(1,0),(1,1)$. Every feasible point can be expressed as $(x,y)=(1-x)(0,0)+(x-y)(1,0)+y(1,1)$, with nonnegative coefficients summing to1.

Its objective is therefore a convex combination of the vertex values $0,a,a+b$, so at least one vertex maximizes the objective. Comparing these values gives the stated conditions.

Because $a,b\neq0$, the middle vertex is uniquely optimal exactly when $a>0,b<0$. For the origin, strict uniqueness requires $a<0,a+b<0$; for $(1,1)$ it requires $b>0,a+b>0$.

At $a+b=0$ with $a<0<b$, every point on the diagonal edge from $(0,0)$ to $(1,1)$ is optimal as well. Thus existence of a vertex optimum does not imply that every optimum is a vertex.
